narrative:
The model estimates a 40% chance that you will fail your final year. That is not a certainty, but it is high enough under the school’s rule to treat you as needing remedial courses. In practical terms, roughly four in ten students with a similar profile would not pass, so the decision is to provide extra support now rather than wait until the end of the year.

The strongest reason is your history of past class failures: you have two, compared with an average of zero among students who passed. This was the top influence and it pushed the prediction clearly toward failing. The next two factors worked in your favor, but only modestly: coming from a family of three or fewer and not having attended nursery school each nudged the estimate toward passing, so they reduced risk slightly rather than caused the failure prediction. The model still treated the repeated-failure signal as more important than those protective factors. Your low absences—two, below the average of about 3.8—are also a positive sign.

To improve your chances, focus on breaking the pattern behind past failures. Meet your teachers or tutor early, use structured remedial classes, and set a weekly study plan; your family support and internet access can help. Consider increasing study time beyond the current two-to-five hours and protecting time for coursework, especially if going out with friends is high. Remedial courses should be used as targeted help to change the outcome, not as a fixed label.
